\chapter{Not That, and Neither}
\label{ch:ka-not-that}
\hlchaptermodality{68}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can deny that something is what you called it, disagree politely, and say that I do not know either.}

Complete KA-C68-me-neither and use both Kannada negatives correctly in one exchange.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[a]{\kn{ಅ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:KA-S135-letter-a}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \kn{ಮ} — what sound does it carry?

One character this time — and the first one in this book that arrives with instructions.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \kn{ಅ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಅ}} — \emph{a}.

It is an \textbf{independent vowel} — the shape \emph{a} takes when a word begins with it, rather than the sign it becomes inside one.

You already say these, and every one of them has \kn{ಅ} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಅಥವಾ}} \emph{athavā} — or, from two lessons ago
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಅಲ್ಲಿ}} \emph{alli} — there, where I am not
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಅಜ್ಜ}} \emph{ajja} — grandfather
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಅತಿಥಿ}} \emph{atithi} — a guest
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \kn{ಅ}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} turn clockwise around the compact left loop
  \item \textbf{2.} sweep around the broad lower bowl
  \item \textbf{3.} turn counterclockwise around the rounded right loop
  \item \textbf{4.} return left along the inward horizontal bar
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 0.} The pen stays down from the first movement to the last.

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — Kannada handwriting is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Gopala Krishna A, 'Kannada-alphabet-a.gif', 35 frames, Wikimedia Commons, 25 May 2016, CC BY-SA 4.0.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
Every character before this one asked you only to copy what you could see, because nothing available to this book said where the pen starts. For \kn{ಅ} somebody wrote it down and published it, so here it is. The characters still waiting on a source keep the older instruction, and will until one turns up.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \kn{ಅ} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\kn{ಅಥವಾ}  ·  \kn{ಅಲ್ಲಿ}  ·  \kn{ಅಜ್ಜ}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \kn{ಅ} three times, saying \emph{a} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \kn{ಅ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \kn{ಅ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{a}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[alla]{\kn{ಅಲ್ಲ} (alla) — is not}

\label{lesson:KA-C68-is-not}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: which character did you trace last, and what does \emph{illa} deny?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಅಲ್ಲ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಅಲ್ಲ}} (\emph{alla}) — \textquotedblleft{}is not (that)\textquotedblright{}.

Since the very first chapter you have had \kn{ಇಲ್ಲ} (\emph{illa}). One letter apart, and a different job entirely.

\textbf{\kn{ಪುಸ್ತಕ} \kn{ಇಲ್ಲ}} (\emph{pustaka illa}) — \textquotedblleft{}there is no book.\textquotedblright{} Nothing of that kind is here.

\textbf{\kn{ಇದು} \kn{ಪುಸ್ತಕ} \kn{ಅಲ್ಲ}} (\emph{idu pustaka alla}) — \textquotedblleft{}this is not a book.\textquotedblright{} The thing is here; the description is wrong.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two negatives, and which one to reach for}]
Kannada splits the negative in two, and neither half can do the other's work. \kn{ಇಲ್ಲ} denies that something \textbf{is there}. \kn{ಅಲ್ಲ} denies that something \textbf{is that}.

English hides the split behind one word — \textquotedblleft{}there is no book\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}this is not a book\textquotedblright{} — and a learner who reaches for \kn{ಇಲ್ಲ} in the second sentence has said something a Kannada speaker cannot make sense of. The test is simple: if you could point at the thing, you need \kn{ಅಲ್ಲ}.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
This is also how you disagree. Kannada has no everyday sentence for \textquotedblleft{}I disagree\textquotedblright{}; what a speaker says is that the description is wrong.

\textbf{\kn{ಅದು} \kn{ನಿಜ} \kn{ಅಲ್ಲ}} (\emph{adu nija alla}) — \textquotedblleft{}that is not true.\textquotedblright{}

Notice what it does not do: it contradicts the statement and leaves the person out of it. Said flatly it is firm; said with \kn{ಸ್ವಲ್ಪ} or a softening \kn{ಇಲ್ಲ} in front of it, it is gentle. Both are ordinary.
\end{culture}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A second negative, and the first way to disagree.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{alla}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{pustaka illa}, then \emph{idu pustaka alla}, and say which one denies a description
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{adu nija alla}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{athavā}, then say \emph{nānū}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{mattu} once more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{\kn{ಮ}} once more
  \item \emph{Recall:} from much earlier — say \emph{kurci}, \emph{bāgilu}, \emph{hoṭṭe}, \emph{beraḷu}, and say what each one means
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{hullu}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which negative denies that a thing exists? (\emph{illa}.) Which one denies that it is what you called it? (\emph{alla}.) Disagree with something, out loud.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hālū illa, nīrū illa]{\kn{ಹಾಲೂ} \kn{ಇಲ್ಲ}, \kn{ನೀರೂ} \kn{ಇಲ್ಲ} (hālū illa, nīrū illa) — neither milk nor water}

\label{lesson:KA-C68-neither}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: which negative would you use to say \textquotedblleft{}this is not a book\textquotedblright{}?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಹಾಲೂ} \kn{ಇಲ್ಲ}, \kn{ನೀರೂ} \kn{ಇಲ್ಲ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಹಾಲೂ} \kn{ಇಲ್ಲ}, \kn{ನೀರೂ} \kn{ಇಲ್ಲ}} (\emph{hālū illa, nīrū illa}) — \textquotedblleft{}there is neither milk nor water.\textquotedblright{}

Nothing here is new. It is the \textquotedblleft{}both\textquotedblright{} ending from the \kn{ನಾನೂ} lesson — \textbf{-\kn{ೂ}} on each of the two nouns — with \kn{ಇಲ್ಲ} after each one instead of nothing.

Kannada builds \textquotedblleft{}neither … nor\textquotedblright{} out of \textquotedblleft{}both … and\textquotedblright{} plus a negative, and it says the negative twice. English says it once and marks the pair with \emph{neither}; Kannada marks the pair with the ending and lets each half deny itself.

You can hear the shape in the shorter version a shopkeeper would actually use: \textbf{\kn{ಹಾಲೂ} \kn{ನೀರೂ} \kn{ಇಲ್ಲ}} — the ending on both, the denial once at the end.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
And, or, but, both — and now neither. The whole of the joining ending's range in two lessons.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{hālū nīrū} — both
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{hālū illa, nīrū illa} — neither
  \item \emph{Say it:} pick two things in this room and deny both of them
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{alla}, then say what it denies that \emph{illa} does not
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{athavā} once more
  \item \emph{Recall:} from much earlier — say \emph{raṅgōli}, \emph{kūdalu}, \emph{hallu}, \emph{kālu}, and say what each one means
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\kn{ಭತ್ತ}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which ending marks the pair? (\textbf{-\kn{ೂ}}.) How many times does \kn{ಇಲ್ಲ} get said in the full form? (Twice.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[gottilla]{\kn{ಗೊತ್ತಿಲ್ಲ} (gottilla) — I don't know}

\label{lesson:KA-C68-dont-know}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what does \emph{gottu} mean on its own?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಗೊತ್ತಿಲ್ಲ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಗೊತ್ತಿಲ್ಲ}} (\emph{gottilla}) — \textquotedblleft{}(it) is not known\textquotedblright{}, and in practice \textquotedblleft{}I don't know\textquotedblright{}.

Both halves have been sitting in this book for chapters. \kn{ಗೊತ್ತು} (\emph{gottu}, \textquotedblleft{}known\textquotedblright{}) came with the core verbs; \kn{ಇಲ್ಲ} came on page one. Push them together and the vowel between them drops out: \kn{ಗೊತ್ತು} + \kn{ಇಲ್ಲ} $\to$ \kn{ಗೊತ್ತಿಲ್ಲ}.

The full sentence keeps the dative you learned for knowing: \textbf{\kn{ನನಗೆ} \kn{ಗೊತ್ತಿಲ್ಲ}} (\emph{nanage gottilla}) — literally \textquotedblleft{}to me it is not known\textquotedblright{}. Knowing happens \textbf{to} you in Kannada, and so does not knowing.

On its own, \kn{ಗೊತ್ತಿಲ್ಲ} is a complete and perfectly polite answer.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The most useful three syllables an A1 speaker owns.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{gottu}, then \emph{gottilla}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{nanage gottilla}
  \item \emph{Say it:} ask yourself something you do not know the answer to, and answer it
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \textquotedblleft{}neither milk nor water\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ādare} once more
  \item \emph{Recall:} from much earlier — say \emph{uppu}, \emph{dīpa}, \emph{baṭṭe}, \emph{haṇṇu}, and say what each one means
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{beḷe}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಗೊತ್ತಿಲ್ಲ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}I don't know\textquotedblright{}.) Which two words is it made of? (\emph{gottu} and \emph{illa}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nanagū gottilla]{\kn{ನನಗೂ} \kn{ಗೊತ್ತಿಲ್ಲ} (nanagū gottilla) — I don't know either}

\label{lesson:KA-C68-me-neither}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: how do you say you don't know?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ನನಗೂ} \kn{ಗೊತ್ತಿಲ್ಲ}}
\textbf{\kn{ನನಗೂ} \kn{ಗೊತ್ತಿಲ್ಲ}} (\emph{nanagū gottilla}) — \textquotedblleft{}I don't know either\textquotedblright{}, or plainly \textquotedblleft{}me neither\textquotedblright{}.

The ending you have been hanging on nouns goes on the dative just as happily: \kn{ನನಗೆ} (\emph{nanage}, \textquotedblleft{}to me\textquotedblright{}) becomes \kn{ನನಗೂ} (\emph{nanagū}, \textquotedblleft{}to me as well\textquotedblright{}). Nothing else changes.

Say \kn{ನಾನೂ} and you add yourself to something somebody is doing. Say \kn{ನನಗೂ} and you add yourself to something happening \textbf{to} them — knowing, liking, not knowing. The dative sentences you already own take the second one.

This is the turn a short exchange needs most and almost never gets taught: one person shrugs, and you agree with the shrug.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five ways of joining, and the first that joins you to another person's answer.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{nanage gottilla}, then \emph{nanagū gottilla}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{nānū}, then \emph{nanagū}, and say which one goes with knowing
  \item \emph{Say it:} somebody says \emph{nanage gottilla} — reply
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{alla}, then disagree with something out loud
  \item \emph{Recall:} from much earlier — say \emph{hūmāle}, \emph{heṇḍati}, \emph{gaṇḍa}, \emph{ajji}, and say what each one means
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\kn{ಸುಗ್ಗಿ}}, then say \emph{mattu}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ನನಗೂ} \kn{ಗೊತ್ತಿಲ್ಲ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}I don't know either\textquotedblright{}.) Which ending made it \emph{either}? (\textbf{-\kn{ೂ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
